title: Regularity and projectivity of a point blowup on a regular surface
statement: Let $X$ be an integral regular excellent Noetherian scheme of dimension $2$ admitting an ample invertible sheaf. Let $p\in X$ be closed with $\dim\mathcal O_{X,p}=2$, and let $b:X'=\operatorname{Bl}_pX\to X$ be the blowup of the reduced closed point. Then $X'$ is integral regular excellent Noetherian of dimension $2$ and admits an ample invertible sheaf. The morphism $b$ is of finite type and projective in the finite-projective-space convention. Its exceptional divisor $E=b^{-1}(p)$ is isomorphic to $\mathbf P^1_{\kappa(p)}$ and is regular. For any closed subscheme $W\subseteq X$ containing $p$, the support of $W\times_XX'$ is the union of $E$ and the support of the strict transform of $W$. For any integral closed subscheme $Y\subseteq X$, its strict transform is the blowup of $Y$ in $p\times_XY$. Conventions: [def-pc-integral-scheme], [def-weil-regular-scheme], [def-exc-excellent-ring], [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring], [def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring], [def-weil-pbc-ample-invertible-module], [def-nagata-global-blowup], [def-weil-closed-immersion], [def-nagata-strict-transform], [def-kun-projective], [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], [def-nagata-projective-space-base-change], [def-weil-residue-field], [def-pc-fibre-product].

proof.text: Let $\mathcal I$ be the ideal sheaf of the reduced closed point $p$. The closed-immersion ideal-sheaf description makes it quasi-coherent. On an affine $\operatorname{Spec}R$ containing $p$ it is the maximal ideal of $p$, and on an affine not containing $p$ it is the unit ideal. Each is finitely generated because $R$ is Noetherian; thus $\mathcal I$ is of finite type. It is nonzero: at $p$, its stalk is the maximal ideal of the two-dimensional regular local ring, which cannot be zero (a field has dimension zero).

source.place: Preparation for quadratic transformations; reduced-point ideal

proof.text: Apply the integral finite-type blowup theorem to $(X,\mathcal I)$: $X\prime$ is integral and $b$ is projective in the projective-bundle sense. Since $X$ has an ample invertible sheaf, the projective-bundle-to-H-projective theorem gives a closed immersion into a finite projective space over $X$, as required. The blowup properness theorem makes $b$ proper, hence of finite type by the definition of properness. Finite type over the Noetherian scheme $X$ makes $X\prime$ Noetherian. On an excellent affine open $\operatorname{Spec}R\subseteq X$, choose finite generators of the centre ideal $I$. Each blowup chart has ring $R[I/a]$, generated over $R$ by the finitely many fractions $i/a$ from those generators. These rings, and their localizations, are excellent by finite-type stability of excellent rings. Hence $X\prime$ is excellent.

source.place: Tags 02ND and 02NS; morphisms.tex Tag 087S; more-algebra.tex Tag 07QU

proof.text: Choose an ample invertible module $M$ on $X$. By step 2 (the integral finite-type blowup theorem) $b$ is projective in the projective-bundle sense. The theorem that a projective-bundle-projective morphism is quasi-projective therefore supplies an invertible $\mathcal O_{X\prime}$-module $N$ that is $b$-relatively ample: $b$ is quasi-compact and $N|_{b^{-1}(V)}$ is ample for every affine open $V\subseteq X$. These are exactly the hypotheses of the relative-to-absolute twisting theorem for $f=b$, together with the ample module $M$ on $X$; it gives an integer $a\geq0$ for which $N\otimes b^*(M^{\otimes a})$ is ample on $X\prime$. This constructs the ample module needed for the next blowup; no ampleness of $b^*M$ alone is asserted.

Put $A=\mathcal O_{X,p}$, with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ and residue field $k=\kappa(p)$. Choose an affine neighbourhood $\operatorname{Spec}R$ of $p$ corresponding to a maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$, so $A=R_{\mathfrak n}$. Localization is flat, and flat base change of blowups identifies $B=\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathfrak m}(\operatorname{Spec}A)$ with $X\prime\times_X\operatorname{Spec}A$. This preserves the fibre over $p$, and every local ring at a point of that fibre: on an affine chart with ring $C$, the base change replaces $C$ by $(R\setminus\mathfrak n)^{-1}C$. A prime $\mathfrak q$ over $\mathfrak n$ avoids these denominators, so $((R\setminus\mathfrak n)^{-1}C)_{\mathfrak q}=C_{\mathfrak q}$. Thus it suffices to compute $B$ along its closed fibre.

source.place: Tags 0805 and 0AGQ: reduction to the local surface

proof.text: Since $A$ is regular local of dimension two, choose generators $x,y$ of $\mathfrak m$. Both orders $(x,y)$ and $(y,x)$ are regular sequences. The blowup chart isomorphisms and the regular-sequence presentation give the covering charts $C_x=A[\mathfrak m/x]=A[t]/(xt-y)$ and $C_y=A[\mathfrak m/y]=A[u]/(yu-x)$. These charts cover because $x,y$ in degree one generate the Rees algebra. In the first chart $\mathfrak m C_x=(x)$, and in the second $\mathfrak m C_y=(y)$. Multiplication by the chart generator is injective: $C_x\subseteq A_x$ and $x$ is a unit in $A_x$, and likewise for $y$. This proves the local nonzerodivisor assertion directly, without assuming regularity of the blowup.

The closed fibre on these charts has coordinate rings $C_x/(x)=k[t]$ and $C_y/(y)=k[u]$. On their overlap $t=y/x$ is invertible and $u=x/y=t^{-1}$. The standard projective-space chart theorem identifies exactly this gluing with $\mathbf P^1_k$, so $E\cong\mathbf P^1_k$ as schemes, not just as sets. The polynomial ring over a field is regular; hence all local rings of $E$, being the prime localizations on these two charts, are regular local. Thus $E$ is regular.

Let $q$ lie on $E$. By the local-ring comparison above, $\mathcal O_{X\prime,q}$ is a prime localization of $C_x$ or $C_y$. It is Noetherian, since $X\prime$ is Noetherian. The appropriate chart generator $g=x$ or $y$ belongs to its maximal ideal and is a nonzerodivisor, and the quotient by $g$ is $\mathcal O_{E,q}$, regular local by the preceding step. Apply regularity lifting from a regular-sequence quotient with the sequence $(g)$. Away from $E$, the blowup-complement isomorphism identifies local rings with those of the regular scheme $X$. All local rings of $X\prime$ are therefore regular local, so $X\prime$ is regular.

For $q\in E$, the dimension formula for a local quotient by one nonzerodivisor gives $\dim\mathcal O_{X\prime,q}=1+\dim\mathcal O_{E,q}$. Since $E$ is covered by spectra of $k[t]$, whose Krull dimension is one, these local dimensions are at most two. At the point $t=0$ the localization $k[t]_{(t)}$ has dimension one: $(0)\subsetneq(t)$ gives a chain of length one and the global dimension bounds it above. Thus one local ring of $X\prime$ has dimension two. Off $E$ all local dimensions are at most $\dim X=2$ by the complement isomorphism. Taking the supremum of all local-ring dimensions proves $\dim X\prime=2$.

source.place: Tag 0AGR proof; algebra.tex Tag 00KW and the polynomial dimension formula

proof.text: Let $W\subseteq X$ be closed and contain $p$, and put $U=X\setminus\{p\}$. The strict transform is a closed subscheme of $W\times_X X\prime$ and agrees with that fibre product over $U$. The support of $W\times_X X\prime$ is $b^{-1}(|W|)$: locally, an ideal $J$ defining $W$ lies in the prime of a point upstairs exactly when its image lies in that prime, equivalently when the contracted prime lies in $V(J)$. Consequently $E=b^{-1}(p)$ lies in this support. Every point of the support outside $E$ is in the strict transform by the agreement over $U$, while the strict transform itself lies in the support of the fibre product. These two inclusions prove the asserted union, including when $W=p$ or $W=X$.

source.place: Tag 0BIC proof, first sentence; support calculation

proof.text: For an integral closed subscheme $Y\subseteq X$, apply the closed-ambient strict-transform theorem to its closed immersion and the blowup of $p$. It identifies the strict transform with $\operatorname{Bl}_{p\times_XY}(Y)$, with its morphism to $X\prime$. This also covers $Y=p$: the pulled-back ideal is zero, its Rees algebra has only degree zero, and its Proj is empty, as is the strict transform of the subscheme contained in the centre. If $Y$ avoids $p$, the pulled-back ideal is the unit ideal and the blowup is $Y$.
